entries.name: Patrick
entries.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
entries.sourcing: Rich. The Library holds his two letters, the Confession and the Letter to the soldiers of Coroticus, in Latin and in English. They are the only first-person texts that survive from fifth-century Ireland.
entries.floorNote: His letters are his own. His dates are not. They are one editor's reckoning, and the old lives of him add details his letters never give.
entries.relationsSummary: Patrick is told within Insular / Irish Monastic Christianity, the entry for the church that grew up after him. Its link to the Gallic monks names his wish to visit the brothers in Gaul. The medieval Irish and Welsh entries name him too.
entries.why: Patrick was a Romano-British captive who became a missionary bishop in Ireland. His two letters are the one sure voice from fifth-century Ireland. Later Irish and Welsh writers place him at the start of their story.
entries.teaser: Ireland, c. 432 to 461 CE. A captive boy from Britain who came back to Ireland as a bishop, and whose two short letters are the only voice we have from its first church.
entries.longDescription:
Patrick tells his own story in the Confession. His father was a deacon named Calpurnius, and his grandfather was a priest. When Patrick was about sixteen, he was taken captive to Ireland with many thousands of others. He served one master for six years. Then he fled to a ship.

In his Letter he calls himself a bishop, appointed by God, in Ireland. He lives among barbarians, he says, as a stranger and an exile for the love of God. In the Confession he writes that he longed to see his family in Britain and the brothers in Gaul. He felt bound in the Spirit to stay.

The same Letter protests to the soldiers of Coroticus. They had cut down his newly baptized converts and carried others off. He sent a priest with a letter, asking them to give up some of the captives. The soldiers jeered. He asks that this Letter be read aloud before Coroticus himself.
voices: Patrick — a Romano-British captive turned missionary bishop, whose Confession and Letter to Coroticus survive in his own Latin
Muirchu — the Irish writer, active about 697, whose Life of Patrick the Library holds beside the letters
entries.legacy:
Later churches kept his name. A Life of Patrick in the Irish Book of Lismore calls him chief apostle of the west of the world, and father of baptism and belief of the men of Ireland. The Welsh History of the Britons counts the years from the birth of Christ to the coming of Patrick among the Scots. A Welsh Life of Carannog says Carannog went to Ireland, Patrick having gone before him. A Welsh Life of David says angels told Patrick of David thirty years before David was born.

These writers add what his letters never say. The History of the Britons says Pope Celestine sent him. White, his editor, finds that the early evidence is against it. The History says he was a swineherd for seven years. Patrick himself says six. Both accounts are told, and neither settles the other.

entries.name: Justinian I
entries.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
entries.sourcing: Rich. The Library holds his Novels, the new laws he issued as emperor, on the shelf of his church. They include laws on bishops, clergy, monks and heretics. The scan reads well in Latin and poorly in Greek.
entries.floorNote: His church policy is judged very differently by different churches. His laws are his own words. The sources that call him a persecutor were written by his opponents.
entries.relationsSummary: Justinian is told within The Byzantine Imperial Church (Justinianic), the entry for the church of his reign. Its links name his laws and his envoys. They reach the Donatists, the Montanists, the Goths and Vandals, the followers of Severus and the Nobadae.
entries.why: Justinian ruled the Roman empire from Constantinople from 527 to 565. He wrote church law for bishops, monks and heretics, and he called the council of 553. Russian writers cite his laws. Coptic writers curse him.
entries.teaser: Constantinople, 527 to 565 CE. An emperor who made laws for the church as freely as for the state, and who is cited as a lawgiver by some and cursed as a persecutor by others.
entries.longDescription:
Justinian ruled from Constantinople from 527 to 565. His Novels are the laws he issued in his own name. Many of them deal with the church. In a preface to Epiphanius, the archbishop of Constantinople, he writes that priesthood and empire are the greatest gifts of God to men. One serves divine things, and the other watches over human things.

In 535 he made a law for Africa, which his armies had won back. It named the Donatists with Jews, pagans and Arians, and barred them from holding services. Another law confirmed the sentence on Severus of Antioch. It ordered his books burned and kept him out of the capital.

In 553 he called a council to condemn the writings of three theologians long dead. He hoped to win back the Miaphysites, and it did not work. His enemies wrote bitterly of him. Procopius says he told the Montanists to give up their beliefs, and that those in Phrygia shut themselves in their churches and burned them.
voices: Justinian — emperor from 527 to 565, whose Novels, the laws issued in his name, the Library holds in Latin and Greek
entries.legacy:
Two later churches name him, and they disagree. In the Russian record of the case against Patriarch Nikon, a reply cites a Novel of his. It says the pope of the elder Rome is first of all the priests, and the bishop of Constantinople second.

The Coptic History of the Patriarchs calls him an evil man and a heretic. It says he tried to make the orthodox return to the faith of Chalcedon, and that he seized the patriarch Severus. It says he was like Nestorius. His own preface speaks of priesthood and empire as God's gifts. The Coptic writers do not credit it.

entries.name: Bede
entries.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
entries.sourcing: Rich. The Library holds his Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation in English, on the shelf of the Anglo-Saxon church and as context on the Irish and Welsh shelves. At its close he lists the other books he wrote.
entries.floorNote: Not in question. One caution applies. His History is the main record of the English church to 732, so what he says of its rivals rests on him alone, and he was not neutral.
entries.relationsSummary: Bede is told within Anglo-Saxon Christianity, whose best-known voice he is. Two of its links to the Britons carry his own words. Its other links use his History as their witness. There he is the source, not the subject.
entries.why: Bede was a monk of Jarrow. He wrote the History of the English church. Wycliffite writers cite him against clerical greed. The Roman Breviary gives him a feast.
entries.teaser: Jarrow, c. 673 to 735 CE. A monk given to his monastery at seven, who wrote the book that is still the main record of the English church.
entries.longDescription:
Bede was born about 673 on land that belonged to the monastery at Wearmouth and Jarrow. At seven he was given to Abbot Benedict to be educated, and later to Ceolfrid. He says he spent the rest of his life in that monastery.

He became a deacon at nineteen and a priest at thirty. He wrote that he always took delight in learning, teaching and writing. His History was addressed to King Ceolwulf, who had asked to read it. He finished it about 731.

He died on Ascension Day in 735, aged sixty-two. His pupil Cuthbert described the scene at his deathbed. Bede had just finished translating the Gospel of John.
voices: Bede — monk and priest of Wearmouth and Jarrow, whose Ecclesiastical History of the English Nation the Library holds in English
entries.legacy:
Two later traditions name him. A Wycliffite English tract warns priests who say Mass in pride and greed. It cites Saint Bede, who says we sell Christ when we forsake truth and take up falsehood.

The Roman Breviary keeps his feast on 27 May as Confessor and Doctor of the Church. Its lessons quote him saying that brighter times never shone on England than under Theodore. The Missal has a prayer that thanks God for lighting the church by the learning of blessed Bede.

Bede: Cuthbert's letter on Bede's death, vendored, so the deathbed sentence rests on the primary account and not on Jane's 1903 biographical notice.
flags: Dates. Patrick: 'c. 432-461' follows White 1920 (consecration 432, death 461 by 'the most recent calculations'); the letters give no dates and the old tradition differs (Nennius gives him 120 years).
